body:
Where and Why the Movement Occurred

The Borsad Satyagraha took place during 1923–1924 in a part of Gujarat that then belonged to Kheda district. Borsad is now in Anand district.

The colonial administration decided to impose an additional tax to pay for a special police presence in an area affected by armed robberies and related law-and-order problems. Residents objected because they considered it unjust to make the wider population bear this punitive cost.

The government announced the levy on 25 September 1923. The dispute ultimately involved 104 villages.

Punitive police tax

A punitive police tax is an additional levy imposed on a population to meet the cost of special policing or as a penalty associated with alleged disturbances or insecurity. It is different from ordinary agricultural land revenue.

Inquiry and Leadership

After complaints from villagers, the Gujarat Prantik Samiti appointed Ravishankar Maharaj and Mohanlal Pandya to investigate the grievance.

The committee's findings were considered at a meeting in Borsad on 1 December 1923. The organization decided to begin satyagraha and entrusted its leadership to Vallabhbhai Patel.

Patel organized resistance to the additional tax. The campaign depended on local cooperation, the collection of information about the grievance and the willingness of residents to refuse payment despite official pressure.

Outcome

The movement achieved its immediate objective. On 8 January 1924, the government abolished the additional punitive tax imposed on the 104 affected villages. It also announced the return of amounts already collected and property that had been attached in connection with the levy.

The Borsad campaign reinforced Patel's reputation as an effective organizer of disciplined, nonviolent public resistance.

Distinction from Kheda

Although Borsad and Kheda are geographically and politically connected, their immediate grievances were different. Kheda in 1918 concerned the demand for relief from agricultural land revenue after crop failure. Borsad in 1923 concerned an additional police tax imposed on local residents.

Prelims focus

  • 1923–1924: Borsad Satyagraha.
  • Leader: Vallabhbhai Patel.
  • Cause: An additional punitive police tax.
  • Inquiry: Ravishankar Maharaj and Mohanlal Pandya.
  • 8 January 1924: Tax abolished for 104 villages.
  • Trap: Borsad was not a movement against a 22% rise in land revenue; that was the issue at Bardoli.

[Sources: Government of India, Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook: Anand, “Brief History of the District”, pp. 14–15; Sardar Patel Trust, “His Journey”, entries for 1923–1924. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Kheda in 1918 contested land revenue after crop failure; Borsad in 1923–1924 contested punitive police tax, withdrawn on 8 January 1924 for 104 villages.
pictures.caption: The different taxation grievances behind Kheda and Borsad.

title: Borsad Satyagraha of 1923–1924: Resistance to a Punitive Police Tax

body:
Background of the Revenue Dispute

Bardoli, in present-day Surat district, Gujarat, became the centre of a major peasant satyagraha in 1928.

The colonial government imposed an increase of approximately 22% in land-revenue assessment. Farmers considered the increase unjust, particularly because agricultural conditions and their capacity to pay did not justify the additional burden.

Unlike the Ahmedabad mill struggle, Bardoli involved cultivators rather than industrial wage workers. Unlike Borsad, the disputed payment was an increase in agricultural land revenue, not a special police tax.

Patel's Leadership

The farmers sought the leadership of Vallabhbhai Patel. Before organizing the campaign, Patel examined the grievance and assessed whether the peasants could maintain a disciplined struggle.

He then organized the villages for collective nonpayment of the revised revenue demand. The movement depended on coordinated local action rather than isolated refusals by individual farmers.

How the Movement Was Organized

  • Village organization: Local workers and committees maintained contact with cultivators.
  • Collective discipline: Participants were encouraged to remain united and resist pressure without violence.
  • Communication: Messages, reports and publications, including the Bardoli Satyagraha Patrika, helped sustain the campaign.
  • Acceptance of consequences: Farmers were prepared to face attachment of property and other official measures rather than voluntarily submit to the disputed increase.
  • Negotiation: The movement maintained pressure for reconsideration of the revenue assessment.

These methods made Bardoli an important example of Patel's ability to turn a local grievance into a well-organized mass movement.

Result and the Title Sardar

The government eventually withdrew the disputed increase and accepted reconsideration of the revenue assessment. The campaign was widely regarded as a success for the cultivators.

During the Bardoli movement, the people honoured Vallabhbhai Patel with the title Sardar, meaning leader or chief. The title became permanently associated with him.

The central association

Bardoli + 1928 + 22% land-revenue increase + Vallabhbhai Patel + title Sardar form one connected set of facts.

Prelims focus

  • 1928: Bardoli Satyagraha.
  • Location: Bardoli, present-day Surat district, Gujarat.
  • Issue: Approximately 22% increase in land revenue.
  • Leader: Vallabhbhai Patel.
  • The people of Bardoli honoured Patel with the title Sardar.
  • Trap: Patel received the title Sardar in connection with Bardoli, not the earlier Kheda campaign.

[Sources: Government of India, Central Bureau of Communication, Mann Ki Baat, October 2025, p. 44; Press Information Bureau, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel: The Man Who United the Nation, 30 October 2021, pp. 1–2; Press Information Bureau, “Sardar Patel: Organiser par excellence”, section on Bardoli, 2016. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Patel's leadership, village teams, communication and discipline sustained Bardoli's collective nonpayment, leading to withdrawal of the disputed 22% increase.
pictures.caption: Local organization helped Bardoli's farmers sustain collective resistance.

title: Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928: Vallabhbhai Patel Becomes Sardar

body:
Why Salt Became a National Issue

Under British rule, the government controlled the manufacture and sale of salt and imposed a tax on it. Salt was an essential commodity used by people of every income group.

Gandhi selected the salt law for protest because it connected the wider demand for independence with a burden experienced in everyday life. The salt tax could be understood by farmers, labourers, traders and households across India.

The March from Sabarmati Ashram

On 12 March 1930, Gandhi left Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad with 78 selected companions. The destination was the coastal village of Dandi, now in Navsari district, Gujarat.

The march covered more than 240 miles, or approximately 385 kilometres, over 24 days. People gathered along the route to hear Gandhi explain the purpose of the campaign.

On 6 April 1930, Gandhi deliberately violated the colonial salt law at Dandi by making salt from seawater. The action became the symbolic opening of the Civil Disobedience Movement.

Why Breaking the Salt Law Was Different from Boycott

Non-Cooperation means withdrawing cooperation from the colonial system. During the earlier Non-Cooperation Movement, people were encouraged to boycott foreign cloth, government-controlled educational institutions and certain colonial institutions.

Civil disobedience goes a step further: participants openly and deliberately break an unjust law while maintaining nonviolent discipline and accepting the consequences.

The Dandi action was therefore not merely a boycott of government salt. It was the deliberate violation of the law governing salt production.

Do not confuse the 2 methods

Non-Cooperation: Refusal to assist or participate in colonial institutions and activities.
Civil Disobedience: Open, nonviolent violation of an unjust colonial law, such as the salt law.

Impact of the March

The action at Dandi inspired salt-law violations and other forms of civil disobedience in different parts of India. The movement brought broader participation from women and other sections of society.

Gujarat's importance was direct: Sabarmati was the starting point, and Dandi was the place where the symbolic breach of the salt law occurred.

Prelims focus

  • 12 March 1930: Gandhi began the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram.
  • He was accompanied at the start by 78 volunteers.
  • The march lasted 24 days and covered more than 240 miles.
  • 6 April 1930: Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi.
  • Dandi is in present-day Navsari district, Gujarat.
  • Trap: The Dandi March began at Sabarmati; it did not begin at Dandi or Kochrab.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, “Nationalism in India”, pp. 62–65; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, “The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947”, p. 121, 2020–21 printing; Government of Gujarat, Navsari District Administration, “Culture and Heritage: Dandi Heritage”; Gandhi Heritage Portal, event chronology for 12 March–6 April 1930. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The important dates, participants and destination of the Dandi Salt March.

pictures.alt: Villagers in khadi clothing gather salt into woven baskets and tend shallow salt pans beside the Arabian Sea during the 1930 Dandi salt protest.

title: Dandi Salt March of 1930: From Sabarmati to Civil Disobedience

body:
Early Life and Entry into Public Work

Vallabhbhai Patel was born on 31 October 1875 at Nadiad, Gujarat. His family home and much of his early life were associated with Karamsad. He trained as a lawyer and established a successful legal practice before entering public life.

Patel joined the Gujarat Sabha in 1915 and came into closer contact with Gandhi through public activities in Gujarat. He became active in local civic work and assisted Gandhi in the Kheda Satyagraha of 1918.

Patel's contribution was especially important in converting political decisions into organized action. He coordinated local workers, maintained discipline and dealt with the practical difficulties faced by participants.

Two Connected Areas of Leadership

Leadership in Public Movements

  • Kheda, 1918: Worked with Gandhi in organizing peasants seeking relief from land-revenue collection.
  • Borsad, 1923–1924: Led resistance to an additional punitive police tax.
  • Bardoli, 1928: Led the campaign against a 22% increase in land revenue and acquired the title Sardar.

Ahmedabad Municipal Administration

Patel was active in Ahmedabad's municipal affairs and served as President of the Ahmedabad Municipal Board from 1924 to 1928. His work emphasized practical public services, including:

  • Improvement of sanitation and cleanliness.
  • Attention to drainage and water supply.
  • Public health and better management of civic services.
  • Personal participation in cleanliness work to encourage public responsibility.

In 1927, Patel also organized relief efforts following severe flooding in Gujarat.

These activities show that his public career was not confined to protest. He also gained experience in local administration and the organization of essential services.

Leadership in the Indian National Congress

Patel became an important national leader of the Congress and was elected its President at the Karachi Session in 1931. His reputation rested on disciplined organization, practical judgment and the ability to maintain unity in difficult campaigns.

Prelims focus

  • 31 October 1875: Patel's accepted birth date; birthplace Nadiad.
  • Karamsad: His family home and an important centre of his early life.
  • 1918: Major role in the Kheda Satyagraha.
  • 1924–1928: President of the Ahmedabad Municipal Board.
  • 1931: President of the Congress at its Karachi Session.
  • Trap: Nadiad was Patel's birthplace; Karamsad was his family home.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel: The Man Who United the Nation, 30 October 2021, pp. 1–2; Press Information Bureau, “Sardar Patel: Organiser par excellence”, sections on Ahmedabad municipality and Bardoli, 2016; Sardar Patel Trust, “His Journey”, entries for 1875 and 1915–1931. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Patel combined nonviolent campaigns in Kheda, Borsad and Bardoli with Ahmedabad civic work and Gujarat flood relief, then became Congress President in 1931.
pictures.caption: Patel's leadership combined mass movements with municipal administration.

title: Vallabhbhai Patel: Public Leadership, Organization and Civic Service
